question: Can a reusable proof framework turn first-step gradient alignment into end-to-end learning guarantees for two-layer networks beyond the fixed-kernel regime?

key_findings.claim: The framework defines useful gradient features as directions that a nontrivial fraction of randomly initialized neurons' population gradients align with.
key_findings.evidence: At near-zero symmetric output, first-layer gradients depend mainly on label-weighted input moments. If enough neurons fall in cones around task directions and a small target network can be expressed with those post-step features, later second-layer optimization can achieve low population loss.

key_findings.claim: The main theorem separates feature emergence, existence of a sparse good predictor over learned features, and optimization/generalization of output weights.
key_findings.evidence: Under symmetric Gaussian initialization, boundedness, smoothness, width, sample, and step-size conditions, one large first-layer step creates task-aligned activations. Subsequent updates primarily fit second-layer coefficients; the guarantee is explicit but parameter dependencies can be large and problem-specific.

key_findings.claim: Applications prove learning of structured Gaussian mixtures and parity families where fixed initialization features or NTK require worse complexity.
key_findings.evidence: For mixtures, initial gradients identify component mean directions; for block parities, gradients expose parity-related features under a specially constructed distribution. Propositions compare against finite and infinite fixed-feature maps, demonstrating a separation in the chosen regimes rather than universal NTK inferiority.

key_findings.claim: The lottery-ticket interpretation locates sparse useful subnetworks after the first gradient step, not necessarily at initialization.
key_findings.evidence: The learned feature set contains enough aligned neurons that sparse second-layer weights can form a good predictor, and training such a subset can achieve similar loss. This differs from the classic claim of trainable subnetworks already present with their original initialization and does not give a practical ticket-finding algorithm for deep nets.

method.core_idea: Reduce nonlinear network learning to whether early population gradients create a sufficiently rich, task-aligned feature dictionary.
method.mechanism: Use zero-output symmetric initialization, characterize cone-aligned first-layer gradients, take a feature-learning step, prove existence of a sparse target over resulting ReLUs, optimize second-layer weights, control finite-sample deviations, and instantiate the template for Gaussian mixtures and parity distributions.
assumptions: A two-layer ReLU network with symmetric initialization represents the relevant phenomenon.
Population gradients have a task-aligned cone of nonnegligible probability.
One or a few large early steps expose the needed features.
The learned feature dictionary contains a bounded sparse approximator.
Fresh samples or concentration assumptions support population-to-empirical transfer.

techniques.role: Formalizes task directions visible in initial gradients.
Separates nonlinear feature movement from convex coefficient fitting.
Constructs regimes where learned features beat fixed ones.
Extracts a sparse good subnetwork after feature emergence.

evaluations.metric: Population classification loss and sample/width complexity
evaluations.result: Theorems guarantee recovery through mean-aligned gradient features
evaluations.baseline: Random fixed features and NTK-style methods

evaluations.result: Gradient feature learning achieves arbitrarily small error under stated polynomial conditions
A specialized analysis provides a guarantee under stronger construction
Useful sparse readout exists after the first feature step

limitations: The framework targets two-layer networks and crafted distributions.
Symmetric zero-output initialization and staged learning simplify real joint training.
Polynomial/exponential constants and width bounds may be far from practical.
The parity signal is built into distributional moments visible to gradients.
No deep-network experiment tests whether the sufficient conditions diagnose real tasks.
failure_modes: Initial gradients cancel and reveal no target direction.
Useful features require many sequential representation changes.
Finite-sample noise overwhelms rare aligned neurons.
Feature movement destroys previously learned directions during joint training.
A fixed kernel is already sufficient, making the extra machinery unnecessary.
Deep compositional features cannot be represented by one hidden layer.
reusable_insights: Factor feature-learning proofs into gradient visibility, approximation, optimization, and generalization lemmas.
State separations against the exact fixed-feature class being ruled out.
Analyze useful subnetworks before and after early feature motion separately.
Turn sufficient conditions into measurable diagnostics on real training.
Report sample, width, and step-size dependencies rather than only asymptotic success.
open_questions: Can gradient-feature sets compose across many layers?
Do measured initial gradients predict features learned by practical networks?
How robust are the guarantees to label noise and correlated nuisance features?
Can multiple moderate steps replace the staged large-step proof?
Can the framework yield realistic rates on convolutional or transformer architectures?

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Feature Learning with One Gradient Step in Two-Layer Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This work also studies how one gradient step learns task-aligned features in two-layer networks. The reviewed framework emphasizes a reusable gradient-feature condition and applications spanning Gaussian mixtures, parity, kernel separation, and post-step lottery tickets.

competitive_landscape.title: Hidden Progress in Deep Learning: SGD Learns Parities Near the Computational Limit
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbe et al. analyze SGD learning parity and hidden progress near computational thresholds. The present paper places a structured parity case inside a more general gradient-feature template and contrasts learned with fixed features.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Hu characterize infinite-width parameterizations that do or do not learn features. This paper gives finite two-layer sufficient conditions and task-specific sample/width guarantees centered on early gradients.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: NTK freezes the effective feature map at initialization in the infinite-width lazy regime. The reviewed work constructs tasks where moving first-layer weights along gradient features yields provable advantages over that class.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A unified gradient-feature principle yields provable neural-network guarantees beyond kernels and explains mixtures, parities, and lottery tickets.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A general theorem modularizes early feature creation and later fitting, followed by long complete proofs for multiple distributions and fixed-feature separations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The framework is a meaningful unification of a growing one-step/early-feature literature. Its explanatory reach is limited by shallow architecture, engineered distributions, initialization, and loose complexity; lottery-ticket language should be qualified as post-step sparse approximation.
